frameworks.name: The Solomon Project
frameworks.definition: A structured dialogue practice in which a founder speaks to their 85-year-old self weekly to gain advice grounded in complete life context and perfectly aligned incentives.

frameworks.name: Knowledge Gap vs. Execution Gap
frameworks.definition: A diagnostic framework distinguishing problems stemming from lack of knowledge from problems stemming from failure to execute known solutions, with different remedies for each.

claims.text: The Solomon Paradox (studied in psychology) describes the phenomenon that people give better advice to others than they follow in their own lives, because they have removed emotions and tensions from the problem when it is not their own.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: removal of emotional entanglement from the advisory process enables clearer reasoning

claims.text: When advising oneself, combining the Solomon Paradox (people give better advice to others) with the principle that 'no one has more context on your life than you do' creates a uniquely powerful advisory combination unavailable from therapists or coaches who lack your full business and personal history.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the self-advisor has comparable business acumen to a professional coach
the founder has spent limited time with therapists/coaches
claims.mechanism: therapists and coaches require extensive context-building time that reduces their advisory efficiency; self-advice eliminates this context gap and misaligned incentive risk
bounded_by: does not apply to founders with limited business experience or self-awareness
does not eliminate the benefit of professional therapeutic relationships for mental health crisis support

claims.text: Therapists and coaches who view their practice as a business with recurring-revenue incentives are incentivized to make clients feel better in the moment rather than solve problems long-term, because solving the problem would cause the client to leave.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: the therapist/coach operates a recurring-revenue business model
client continuation is dependent on ongoing problem existence
claims.mechanism: misaligned incentives (recurring revenue requires client retention) override solution-orientation
bounded_by: does not apply to therapists structured as outcomes-based or crisis-response (e.g., emergency psychiatric care)
does not generalize to all therapists — many operate with genuine patient-benefit intent

claims.text: Self-coaching via dialogue with one's future self provides two advantages no external advisor possesses: complete context on one's situation and perfectly aligned incentives, because only you benefit from your success and suffer from your failure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: no external party has both full information about your life and the same time-horizon incentives you do
bounded_by: assumes the individual has sufficient self-awareness to identify biases
does not replace crisis mental health intervention

claims.text: In weight-loss sales and other domains, when a prospect claims 'I don't know what to do,' the actual problem is usually not knowledge but execution: the prospect knows the solution (exercise, eat better) but lacks accountability to implement it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: high-involvement consumer decision (weight loss, health, business change)
claims.mechanism: emotional friction and lack of accountability prevent action on known solutions; knowledge is not the binding constraint
bounded_by: does not apply to genuinely novel problems where knowledge is actually the constraint

claims.text: The ultimate gift one can give oneself is holding oneself accountable; if you can do this reliably, you can accomplish almost anything, because most people's problems stem from execution failure, not knowledge gaps.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: does not apply to situations where external constraints (severe illness, legal restrictions) bind growth rather than personal discipline

claims.text: When stressed about a business decision or relationship problem, the Solomon Project (weekly dialogue with one's 85-year-old self in a Google Doc) serves as a decision-making razor by making only the few consequential decisions salient while older-self perspective dismisses non-critical worries.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: recurring weekly practice (Hormozi schedules Mondays as the default)
dialogue conducted in low-friction format (Google Doc or chat)
claims.mechanism: older-self perspective (85 years old) provides time-horizon compression that filters noise; older self's stated indifference ('none of this is going to matter') reorients focus to truly binding constraints

claims.text: Wisdom is primarily the result of thinking over a longer time horizon; consulting one's older self is an operationalization of this principle by literally accessing the viewpoint of someone 50+ years forward.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: When older self laughs at younger self's current stress and says 'none of this is going to matter,' it acts as a reframing tool that reduces reactivity in relationships and business decisions by surfacing that most current anxieties are not strategically binding in a multi-decade perspective.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: perspective inflation (treating 12-month panic as insignificant in 85-year view) defuses emotional urgency without dismissing legitimate constraints

examples.text: Hormozi was building a business (billion-dollar scale ambition) while stressed about time-to-outcomes. His older self responded with comic dismissal: 'What did you expect, you're trying to build a billion-dollar thing in what, a year?' This reframing revealed that Hormozi's anxiety about pace was misaligned with the realistic timeline for billion-dollar company construction, allowing him to refocus on leverage-per-unit-time rather than panic about absolute speed.

In a sales conversation about weight loss, a prospect claimed 'I don't know what to do.' Hormozi responded by asking directly, 'If you had to lose weight, what would you do?' The prospect answered: 'I'd probably work out' and 'eat a little better.' Hormozi then surfaced the execution gap: 'Pretty much got it. But that's not the issue, is it? ...It's that you're not doing it.' The prospect acknowledged this. This revealed that the knowledge (exercise + diet) was present but accountability was missing.

When Hormozi began the Solomon Project dialogue with his 85-year-old self, he typed a question about a business decision. His older self responded by asking the same diagnostic questions Hormozi would ask a portfolio company CEO: 'What is the objective?' This revealed that the self-advisor (older Hormozi) had not only complete context but also business acumen equal to or exceeding external coaches, making self-advice more efficient than paying for external advisory.

A prospect in a romantic relationship scenario was described as 'getting beat by her husband once a month' for 'four years' with the husband now claiming 'it's not going to happen again.' The psychological study (cited under Solomon Paradox) asked a third party: 'What do you think that woman should do?' That third party gave advice that 'completely conflicts with how that woman actually lives her life,' demonstrating the gap between external advisory quality and self-application (the woman was the one in the relationship and presumably knew the answer but could not execute on it).

practices.text: Implement a recurring weekly meeting with your future self (Hormozi uses Monday mornings) in a simple low-friction format (Google Doc or chat interface) to conduct a back-and-forth dialogue addressing current stressors and business decisions.

When a client or team member claims 'I don't know what to do,' directly ask them to generate 2-3 solutions themselves ('If you had to solve this, what would you do?') rather than educating them, to surface that knowledge is present and the problem is execution accountability.

In high-stakes decisions, consult the longer time horizon explicitly by asking 'What would my 85-year-old self say this doesn't matter?' to filter noise from signal and reorient focus to decisions with multi-decade impact.
